volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: What can be shaken
figure: The God whose voice shakes the heavens
moment:
At Sinai, God's voice shook the mountain until the people trembled. But the letter to the Hebrews reaches for a greater promise: Yet once more, God says, I will shake not only the earth, but also the heavens. Then the writer stops to read the meaning of that one phrase, yet once more. The shaking, he says, is a sifting. God shakes in order to remove the things that can be shaken — the made things, the temporary scaffolding — so that the things which cannot be shaken are left standing clear.

This is the promise that hangs over every upheaval in this book: the ones that crack open a soul, and the ones that crack open a church. Upheaval is not God losing His grip on the world. It is God clearing the ground. He does not shake what He means to destroy; He shakes what He means to keep — the way you shake a sieve to find the gold, the way a storm strips a tree of everything that was already dead. What falls in the shaking was always going to fall. What remains was always the real thing.
voiceQuote: Yet once more, I will shake not only the earth, but also the heavens.
voiceAttribution: The LORD, quoted in Hebrews — Hebrews 12:26 (WEB)
scriptureText: This phrase, Yet once more, signifies the removing of those things that are shaken... that those things which are not shaken may remain.
weight:
We meet our upheavals as emergencies — something has gone wrong, and the first instinct is to stop the shaking and get back to how it was. But what if the shaking is not the disaster? What if it is the mercy — the only way the temporary things could be sifted out from the permanent ones, in a life or in a church that had quietly let the two blur together?

God shakes what He loves. He lets the false floor give way precisely because He means to leave you standing on the real one. So when the ground moves under you — your certainties, your plans, your church as you have always known it — the truest question is not how do I make this stop, but what is being revealed here that cannot be shaken? Everything that survives the shaking, you may keep forever.

upheaval.thePhase: Before the four phases begin, hear the promise that covers all of them. Every upheaval moves through a shape — disconnect, disorientation, reorientation, reconnect — and God is in each one. The shaking is not random; it has a destination. You are not merely falling; you are being sifted toward what lasts.
upheaval.inYou: The diagnosis, the doubt, the loss that has shaken your private world feels like collapse. But hold it up to this promise: what is being shaken in you is being separated from what cannot be shaken in you. You are not losing your faith; you may be losing the scaffolding around it, so the real thing can finally stand on its own.
upheaval.inTheBody: Churches are shaken too — by decline, by scandal, by a generation walking away, by a reformation no one asked for. The same promise holds for a community: God shakes the institution He means to renew, not the one He means to abandon. What a shaken church loses is rarely the gospel; it is the scaffolding the gospel had been hiding behind.
upheaval.whatRemains: A kingdom that cannot be shaken. When the made things are gone, Christ and His reign remain — the one floor that holds in every earthquake, personal or ecclesial, the thing you were standing on all along without knowing it.
reflection: What is being shaken in my life right now — and what if it is a sifting, not a disaster?
Which of my certainties were scaffolding, and which is the unshakable thing underneath?
Can I trust that God only shakes what He means to keep?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, when everything shakes, steady me with this: You shake what You love, in order to keep it. Sift out of me, and out of my church, whatever was never going to last, and let me find my feet on the one kingdom that cannot be moved. Amen.

notes.primary: Hebrews 12:26-28 (yet once more I will shake; receiving a kingdom that can't be shaken).
notes.tradition: The reading of upheaval as God's recurring pattern of renewal draws on Phyllis Tickle's The Great Emergence (2008), paraphrased and attributed, never quoted.

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: The rummage sale
moment:
Watching the church convulse at the turn of the millennium, Phyllis Tickle reached for an image she credited to an Anglican bishop, Mark Dyer: about every five hundred years, the church holds a giant rummage sale. The hardened shell the faith has grown — its institutions, its certainties, its settled way of answering everything — cracks, and the household hauls its whole attic out onto the lawn to decide what to keep. It has happened, she observed, on a strange recurring beat: the fall of Rome around 500, the splitting of East and West around 1000, the Reformation around 1500, and now.

And every time, two things are born rather than one. A fresh, more vital form of the faith emerges — and the old form it broke from is not destroyed but purified, handed back its life in a leaner shape. Every rummage sale also forces the same unsettling question up out of the basement: where now is the authority? When the old answer cracks, the church has to discover again what it actually stands on. Jesus had drawn the whole picture centuries before, in a single sentence about wine.
voiceQuote: They put new wine into fresh wineskins, and both are preserved.
scriptureText: Don't remember the former things, neither consider the things of old. Behold, I will do a new thing... I will even make a way in the wilderness, and rivers in the desert.
weight:
It is easy to read a rummage sale as a death. The familiar is going out the door; the building feels emptier; the people who loved the old arrangement are grieving, and not without reason. But new wine does not burst old skins because the wine has gone bad. It bursts them because it is alive and expanding, and the old container can no longer hold what God is fermenting.

This does not make the upheaval painless — rummage sales are disruptive, and much that is genuinely precious can be carried out with the junk if no one is watching the table. But it changes the question. A shaken church is not necessarily a dying church; it may be a household making room. So alongside what are we losing, the renewing question is also this: what new thing is God pouring, and which skins will have to change to hold it?

upheaval.thePhase: A rummage sale is the whole four-phase cycle at the scale of a church: the body disconnects from a form it has outgrown, disorients in the clearing-out, reorients around a truer center, and reconnects in a leaner shape. Most shaken churches are somewhere in that cycle without knowing it has a name — or an end.
upheaval.inYou: You hold your own rummage sales. There are seasons when God clears out a faith you have outgrown — the answers that worked at twenty, the certainties that cannot carry your forties — and the emptying feels like loss until you realize it is making room. The clutter of an old faith can crowd out the living thing it was built to hold.
upheaval.inTheBody: If you lead or love a church in transition, hear this: the decline you fear may be a rummage sale, not a funeral. Watch the table carefully, because real treasure does get carried out with the clutter in the chaos — but do not mistake the emptying for the end. God has done this every five hundred years, and every time the wine outlasted the skins.
upheaval.whatRemains: The wine itself — the gospel of Jesus Christ. Skins change every few centuries; the new-covenant wine they were made to hold does not. What cannot be shaken is never the arrangement; it is the Lord the arrangement existed to serve.
reflection: What in my faith might be an old skin God is asking me to release — and what is the wine He is protecting?
When my church changes, do I grieve the gospel, or only the arrangement I was comfortable with?
Where might an emptying in my life actually be God making room?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, when the familiar goes out the door, teach me to tell the wine from the skins. Give me courage for Your rummage sales — in me and in Your church — and faith that what You clear away, You clear to make room for something more alive. Amen.

notes.primary: Matthew 9:17 (new wine, fresh skins); Isaiah 43:18-19 (behold, I will do a new thing).
notes.tradition: The 500-year rummage sale framework is Phyllis Tickle's, in The Great Emergence (2008), building on an observation she credits to Bishop Mark Dyer — paraphrased and attributed, never quoted.

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: Holy discontent
figure: Jeremiah, the fire in the bones
moment:
Jeremiah had had enough. The cost of speaking God's word had been mockery, beatings, a night in the stocks — so he resolved to quit: I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. The resolution lasted about a sentence. The word he tried to swallow became a burning fire shut up in his bones; he grew weary holding it back, and he could not contain it. He could no more stop prophesying than a man can keep his hand in a flame.

That fire has a name. Bill Hybels called it holy discontent, and reached for the cartoon to explain it — Popeye absorbing one indignity too many until he plants his feet and declares he has had all he can stand. It is the God-given inability to accept what is: a wrongness you cannot un-see, a gap between what is and what God intends that you can no longer make your peace with. Jesus had it, braiding a whip of cords in the temple courts while zeal for His Father's house consumed Him. The prophets had it. Luther had it when he had counted the indulgence-sellers' lies one time too many. Every upheaval starts with someone who cannot stand it anymore.
voiceQuote: There is in my heart as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I am weary with forbearing, and I can't contain.
scriptureText: His disciples remembered that it was written, Zeal for your house will eat me up.
weight:
Not all discontent is holy. Most of ours is grumbling, or envy, or wounded pride dressed up as principle, and it builds nothing. But there is a discontent God Himself plants, and it has a different feel: it burns for His glory and for others' good rather than your own, it does not go away when you try to be reasonable, and it costs you something to carry. That fire is often the very first move of God in an upheaval — the spark before the break, the ignition of everything that follows.

The temptation is to put it out. Holy discontent is uncomfortable; it makes you the difficult one, the person who cannot just be grateful and settle down. So we douse it with busyness or cynicism and call that maturity. But before you extinguish the fire in your bones, ask where it came from. The thing you cannot stop caring about, the wrong you cannot accept — God may have lit that, and He may be about to do something with it.

upheaval.thePhase: Holy discontent is the ignition of Disconnect — the first of the four phases. Before anything breaks, someone stops being able to live with the way things are. The crack always comes before the break; the fire in the bones comes before the upheaval it starts.
upheaval.inYou: What is the fire you keep trying to put out? The burden you cannot set down, the injustice that wrecks your sleep, the call you have argued with for years. Test it, because not every itch is holy — but if it burns for God and for others and will not leave you alone, it may be the Lord lighting the fuse of an upheaval your settled life has been avoiding.
upheaval.inTheBody: Reformations begin as holy discontent in the body — one person who will not accept the coldness or the corruption everyone else has normalized. Luther's theses were holy discontent nailed to a door. But the body must discern with care: is this fire for God's honor and the good of His people, or is it one person's will and ego in search of a cause? The discontent that renews a church and the discontent that splits it for nothing can look identical on the first day.
upheaval.whatRemains: God's own holy discontent — the zeal that would not leave sin and death unchallenged, that drove Christ into the temple and finally to the cross. Beneath every true holy discontent burns His, and it does not go out.
reflection: What is the fire shut up in my bones that I keep trying to forbear?
Is my discontent holy — for God and for others — or is it grumbling and wounded pride in disguise?
Where might God be lighting the first spark of an upheaval I have been avoiding?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You know the fire I keep trying to put out. If it is only my own grumbling, quench it. But if it is Your holy discontent, give me courage not to douse what You have lit — and wisdom to carry it for Your glory and the good of Your people. Amen.

notes.primary: Jeremiah 20:9 (a burning fire shut up in my bones); John 2:13-17 (zeal for your house).
notes.tradition: The language of holy discontent, and the Popeye image for it, are from Bill Hybels, Holy Discontent (2007), paraphrased and attributed, never quoted.

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: The four phases
moment:
On the edge of the promised land, Moses tells a whole generation to look back and remember all the way the LORD led them — out of Egypt, through the wilderness, to this very threshold. It was not a straight line, and it was not an accident. It had a shape. There was the night they broke from Egypt and everything familiar fell behind them. There were the long, formless years in the wilderness when they had left the old world but had not yet reached the new one. There was Sinai, where a runaway mob was given a law and a name and became a people. And now there is the land, the reconnection, the arrival into belonging.

Disconnect, disorientation, reorientation, reconnect. Every upheaval — in a soul or in a church — moves through these four phases, and this series will walk them one at a time. The point of naming them is not to make a tidy formula out of pain. It is to tell you, while you are in it, that the chaos has a shape and the road has a destination, and that the same God who went before Israel in cloud and fire is in every phase of yours.
voiceQuote: You shall remember all the way which the LORD your God has led you these forty years in the wilderness, that he might humble you, to prove you, to know what was in your heart.
scriptureText: For everything there is a season, and a time for every purpose under heaven.
weight:
The cruelest thing about an upheaval, while you are inside it, is the feeling that it is shapeless — that you are not on a journey at all, just lost. You cannot see Egypt behind you or the land ahead; you can only see wilderness, and wilderness in every direction looks like being abandoned.

Naming the four phases does not remove the wilderness, but it removes the despair. You are not nowhere; you are somewhere on a known road — past the break, not yet at the arrival, being humbled and proven in the long middle. Israel only saw the shape of their forty years by looking back. You may not see the shape of yours until later either. But it is there, and the God who led every step of theirs is leading every step of yours.

upheaval.thePhase: This entry stands over all four. Disconnect is the break; disorientation is the formless middle; reorientation is the new bearing; reconnect is the arrival into a deeper belonging. The series will take them one at a time — but God leads through all four, and you are always somewhere on the map.
upheaval.inYou: Locate yourself. Has something just broken (disconnect)? Are you wandering with no bearings (disorientation)? Is a new clarity slowly forming (reorientation)? Are you being re-rooted on the far side (reconnect)? Naming your phase will not end it, but it will tell you that you are on a road, not lost in a void.
upheaval.inTheBody: Your church is somewhere on this map too. A community that has just broken with its past, or is wandering in decline, or is finding new bearings, or is settling into a renewed shape — each needs a different word. Much of the anxiety in a shaken church comes from not knowing which phase it is in, and treating wilderness as if it were the end of the road.
upheaval.whatRemains: The God who goes before — the pillar of cloud by day and fire by night. Phases change; the Guide does not. What cannot be shaken is the presence that led Israel through every mile of theirs and has not left the front of your column.
reflection: Which of the four phases am I in right now — and have I been mistaking it for being simply lost?
What would change if I believed my upheaval had a shape and a destination?
Can I trust the God who leads through all four, even where I cannot yet see the road?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I cannot see the shape of what I am in. Remind me that You led Israel out, and through, and in — and that You are leading me the same way. Steady me on the road when all I can see is wilderness. Amen.

notes.primary: Deuteronomy 8:2 (remember all the way the LORD led you); Ecclesiastes 3:1 (a time for every purpose).
notes.tradition: The four-phase map of upheaval — disconnect, disorientation, reorientation, reconnect — applied here to personal and ecclesial change; it resonates with Walter Brueggemann's reading of the Psalms as orientation, disorientation, and new orientation.

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: Disconnect: the break
moment:
The very first word God speaks to Abram is a word of disconnection: go. Leave your country. Leave your relatives. Leave your father's house — every layer of belonging a man could have, peeled away one at a time — and set out for a land that God will show him. Will show him. Not has shown him. The destination is a promise, still over the horizon; the only thing concrete in the command is the leaving.

This is how upheaval begins — not with arrival but with departure, a break from the known before the new is anywhere in sight. The letter to the Hebrews says Abram obeyed and went out, not knowing where he went. That is the signature of the disconnect phase: you move before you can see, you lose the old address before you are given the new one. The faith it requires is not the faith to reach the land; it is the faith to leave Ur.
voiceQuote: Get out of your country, and from your relatives, and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you.
scriptureText: By faith, Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. He went out, not knowing where he went.
weight:
Disconnect is the hardest phase to choose, because it is pure subtraction. You give up the old before you are handed the new; for a while your hands are simply empty. So we try to skip it — to reach a new land while still living at the old address, to be re-formed while clutching the very form God is asking us to release.

It cannot be done. There is no reorientation without disconnection; you cannot be remade while you are gripping the old shape with both hands. The break is not God being cruel; it is God making room. And the faith of this phase is small and enormous at once: to obey the go before you can see the land, trusting that the One who said leave will not leave you.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disconnect — the break, the leaving, the loss of the old before the new appears. What it asks of us: to let go of the known on the strength of a promise we cannot yet see, and to stop trying to reach the new land without leaving Ur.
upheaval.inYou: Your disconnect may be a conviction you cannot un-see, a leaving God is quietly asking of you — a job, a relationship, a comfortable version of faith. The grief of it is real; do not let anyone shame you for grieving. But the call is real too, and the promise travels with you.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church's disconnect is its break with a model that no longer serves — a beloved arrangement, a way of doing things that has become the thing itself. Every reformation is a disconnection, and every disconnection is mourned by someone. Leaders in this phase carry a hard double duty: to honor the grief and still obey the go.
upheaval.whatRemains: The God who calls. Abram lost his country, his kin, his father's house — but not the Voice that spoke. What cannot be shaken in any leaving is the One who goes with you into the unknown and is Himself the inheritance at the end of it.
reflection: What is the Ur God may be asking me to leave before I can see the land?
Where am I trying to be remade while still clutching the old shape with both hands?
Can I trust the One who says leave to not leave me?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You ask me to go before You show me where. Give me Abram's faith — to obey the leaving on the strength of Your promise, to grieve honestly and go anyway, trusting that You who called me will not abandon me on the road. Amen.

notes.primary: Genesis 12:1 (get out of your country); Hebrews 11:8 (he went out, not knowing where he went).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: Disorientation: the wilderness
moment:
In the rubble of his losses, Job does the most human thing: he looks for God. He looks east — nothing. West — he cannot find him. North, south; he works and turns and Job cannot catch a single glimpse of him. The God who once felt so near has gone behind a wall, and Job is left in the worst part of any upheaval: the part after the break, before the new, when the old map of God no longer works and no new one has been drawn.

This is disorientation — the wilderness, the formless middle, the place where the question Phyllis Tickle says every upheaval forces to the surface becomes a personal cry: where now is the authority? What do I trust, when the thing I trusted has cracked? And yet, having searched every empty direction, Job says one defiant, load-bearing thing: but he knows the way that I take. He cannot find God. He has decided that God can still find him.
voiceQuote: If I go east, he is not there; if west, I can't find him; he works to the north, but I can't see him; he turns south, but I can't catch a glimpse of him.
scriptureText: But he knows the way that I take. When he has tried me, I shall come forth like gold.
weight:
Disorientation is the longest and most dangerous phase, because it feels exactly like abandonment. The exodus is over but the land has not appeared; you are in the neutral zone, and every instinct screams that you are simply lost. So we do the two things that wreck people here: we bolt back to Egypt, choosing a familiar bondage over an unbearable uncertainty — or we manufacture a premature, brittle certainty just to make the disorientation stop.

The grace of this phase is hidden, and it is this: God is not lost merely because you cannot find Him. He knows the way you take even when you have lost the map. The wilderness is not God's absence; it is God's furnace, and the gold does not come forth in spite of the fire but because of it. Do not waste your wilderness trying to escape it. Let it try you, and you will come forth like gold.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Disorientation — bearings lost, the old certainties cracked, God seemingly absent, the authority question wide open. What it asks of us: to stay, to not bolt back to Egypt or fake a premature certainty, and to trust the God we cannot presently feel.
upheaval.inYou: This is the phase of doubt, deconstruction, grief, the dark night. Do not mistake God's silence for God's absence; the two feel identical and are not the same. You may not be able to find Him from inside the fog. He has not lost track of you for a second.
upheaval.inTheBody: A disoriented church is declining, fracturing, no longer sure what it believes — stranded between a past that has died and a future not yet born. The danger is the same as the soul's: bolting back to a nostalgic Egypt, or forcing a false, brittle certainty to end the discomfort. The wilderness is doing necessary work; rushing it ruins the gold.
upheaval.whatRemains: The God who knows the way you take. You may lose every bearing; you do not fall off His map. What cannot be shaken in the wilderness is that the One you cannot find has never once failed to find you.
reflection: Where am I tempted to bolt back to a familiar bondage rather than endure the uncertainty?
Am I trying to manufacture a premature certainty just to make the disorientation stop?
Can I rest in this: I cannot find Him, but He knows the way that I take?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have looked in every direction and cannot find You, and the silence frightens me. Hold me in the wilderness when I want to run. Let the fire do its work, and bring me forth like gold — and until then, let it be enough that You know the way that I take. Amen.

notes.primary: Job 23:8-10 (I can't find him; but he knows the way that I take).
notes.tradition: The pivotal upheaval question — where now is the authority? — is Phyllis Tickle's, in The Great Emergence (2008), paraphrased and attributed, never quoted.

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: Reorientation: new bearings
moment:
After the wilderness, a new word. Isaiah paints it as a voice just behind your shoulder, gentle and sure, redirecting you as you walk: this is the way, walk in it — turn neither right nor left. It is not the old certainty handed back unchanged. It is a new bearing, given to people who had genuinely lost their way and have stopped pretending they could find it themselves.

The great picture of this phase is Sinai. A runaway mob of former slaves — disconnected from Egypt, disoriented in the desert — is brought to a mountain and given something they did not have before: a covenant, a law, and a staggering new identity. You shall be my own possession, God says, a kingdom of priests, a holy nation. They went into the wilderness an escaped rabble; they come out of it a people. That is reorientation — not merely surviving the upheaval, but being re-formed by it into something truer than you were before.
voiceQuote: Your ears shall hear a word behind you, saying, This is the way, walk in it.
scriptureText: If you will indeed obey my voice, and keep my covenant, then you shall be my own possession from among all peoples... and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests, and a holy nation.
weight:
Reorientation cannot be rushed, and this is the thing people most want to force. We try to leap from the break straight to the new clarity, skipping the wilderness — and the clarity we manufacture that way is brittle and false. The real thing comes only after disorientation has finished its work, and when it comes you know it: a quiet bearing you could not have engineered, a way forward that simply appears, a faith rebuilt rather than merely restored.

It is rarely the old house put back exactly as it was. It is a new house on the same foundation — leaner, truer, load-tested by the wilderness. The faith on the far side believes fewer things and holds them with far more weight. So when the fog finally lifts a little and you hear the word behind you, do not insist on the old map. Take the new way. It is the gift the wilderness was preparing all along.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Reorientation — the fog lifting enough to find a new bearing, a truer framework forming, a new identity given. What it asks of us: to receive the new way instead of demanding the old certainty back unchanged.
upheaval.inYou: This is reconstruction after deconstruction — faith rebuilt, often smaller and far stronger; a new sense of who you are and what you are for, emerging on the far side of the wilderness. Do not grieve that it is not the old faith returned. It is a truer one, given.
upheaval.inTheBody: A reorienting church is finding new bearings — new forms, a renewed mission, fresh confessions of an old faith. This is where the Reformation's creeds were written and where every renewal movement finds its new shape. The body that endures the wilderness is re-formed by it, not merely returned to what it was.
upheaval.whatRemains: The God who speaks the new way, and the identity He gives — my own possession, a kingdom of priests. What cannot be shaken is that on the far side of the wilderness you are not just rescued; you are renamed.
reflection: Where am I trying to force a premature clarity instead of letting the wilderness finish its work?
Am I willing to take a new way, or only to have my old certainty handed back unchanged?
What new and truer identity might God be forming in me through this upheaval?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, when the fog begins to lift, give me the humility to take the new way and not demand the old one. Re-form me through what I have suffered into something truer than I was. Speak Your word behind me, and let me walk in it. Amen.

notes.primary: Isaiah 30:21 (this is the way, walk in it); Exodus 19:5-6 (my own possession, a kingdom of priests).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: Reconnect: re-rooted
moment:
The far side of an upheaval is not merely the end of the shaking. It is reconnection — and a reconnection deeper than what was lost. In the very middle of the exile's wreckage, with Jerusalem in ruins and the people scattered, Jeremiah hears God promise something better than restoration: a new covenant. Not law carved on stone tablets that can be shattered, but law written on the inward parts, on the heart. I will be their God, and they shall be my people — belonging made interior, unbreakable, closer than it had ever been.

And Scripture's whole story ends on this phase. The last vision is not a return to Eden but something further on: God's tent pitched among His people, no distance left, no veil, no exile — he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them. Every upheaval, rightly traveled, is moving toward this: not back to where you started, but on into a nearer belonging than you had before it all came apart.
voiceQuote: I will put my law in their inward parts, and in their heart will I write it; and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.
scriptureText: Behold, God's tent is with men, and he will dwell with them, and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God.
weight:
Reconnect is the phase we ache for while we are stranded in the other three — and the one we can least manufacture. You cannot arrive on the far side of an upheaval you refused to travel; there is no shortcut from the break to the belonging that skips the wilderness and the slow re-forming. The people who try to force reconnection early only get a counterfeit: the old arrangement propped back up, brittle and unchanged.

But for those who go all the way through — disconnect, disorientation, reorientation — there is a reconnection waiting that is richer than the connection they lost. A faith now written on the inward parts instead of leaning on someone else's stone tablets. A community re-formed and truer than the comfortable one that broke. A belonging the shaking did not destroy but actually deepened. What was torn is not merely repaired. It is remade, and it is closer to God than it ever was before.

upheaval.thePhase: This is Reconnect — re-rooted, integrated, belonging restored and deepened on the far side. What it asks of us: to let the new connection be deeper than the old, rather than settling for the former arrangement propped back up.
upheaval.inYou: The re-rooted faith is interior now — written on your heart, not borrowed from someone else's certainty. You come out of a true upheaval not merely with your faith intact but with it owned, and nearer to God than before the shaking began.
upheaval.inTheBody: A reconnected church is re-membered — communion restored, mission renewed, a body knit back together on the far side of its rummage sale. It is not the old congregation exactly as it was; it is a truer one, and the shaking is part of why.
upheaval.whatRemains: The God who writes Himself on the heart and pitches His tent among His people. What cannot be shaken is the belonging itself — I will be their God, and they shall be my people — the one bond an upheaval can only deepen, never finally break.
reflection: Am I willing to travel all the way through, or am I trying to force an early, counterfeit reconnection?
What might a belonging look like that is deeper than the one I lost?
Where has a past upheaval, fully traveled, actually brought me nearer to God?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, in the middle of the shaking I ache to belong again. Keep me from settling for the old arrangement propped back up. Carry me all the way through to the reconnection You are making — Your law on my heart, Your tent among Your people — and let it be nearer than what I lost. Amen.

notes.primary: Jeremiah 31:33 (a new covenant written on the heart); Revelation 21:3 (God himself will be with them).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: Where now is the authority?
moment:
Phyllis Tickle noticed that every rummage sale drags the same question up out of the basement and sets it on the lawn: where now is the authority? When the old answer cracks — the tradition you inherited, the certainty you were raised on, the leader or the institution or the way of reading the Bible that settled every argument — the church, and the soul, has to discover all over again what it actually stands on. It is a terrifying question while you are inside it. It is also a clarifying one.

Paul had already named the floor beneath every floor. You can lose a hundred lesser authorities — and an upheaval will strip them away one by one — but no one can lay any other foundation than the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ. Jesus said the same thing with a picture: the wise build on rock, and when the floods come and beat against the house, it stands, because of what is underneath it. Upheaval is the flood that finally shows you what your house was built on.
voiceQuote: For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.
scriptureText: Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock... it didn't fall, for it was founded on the rock.
weight:
An upheaval is a flood, and a flood is honest. It does not care what you said your house was built on; it only reveals what it was actually built on. The authorities that wash away in the water were never the foundation, however much weight you had quietly rested on them — a charismatic leader, an unquestioned tradition, a borrowed certainty, your own competence.

This is why the authority question, terrifying as it is, is a gift. It forces you to stop standing on the floors and find the rock. The church that survives its rummage sale is not the one that clings hardest to the old furniture; it is the one that gets driven back down to the one foundation that cannot be relaid or removed. So when the waters rise and your certainties go floating past, ask the clarifying question: under all of it, what am I actually standing on — and is it the rock?

upheaval.thePhase: The authority question belongs to disorientation — the phase where the old map has failed and a new one has not formed. It feels like the worst part. It is often the most important, because it drives you down past every lesser authority to the only one that holds.
upheaval.inYou: Your upheaval will expose what you were really trusting — and it is rarely only Christ. A teacher, a tradition, your own certainty, the feeling of having it figured out. When those wash away, do not despair; you are being driven to the rock that was always underneath, the one the flood cannot move.
upheaval.inTheBody: Every reformation is, at heart, a fight over this question. When a church's old authority cracks, the temptation is to grab the nearest replacement — a stronger leader, a harder line, a nostalgic certainty. The renewing path is harder and surer: back to the one foundation, Christ Himself, beneath every authority the church has ever leaned on.
upheaval.whatRemains: The foundation already laid — Jesus Christ. Every other authority is a floor that can give way; He is the rock the floors were resting on. What cannot be shaken is not your certainty about Him, but Him.
reflection: When my certainties wash away, what am I actually left standing on?
Which authorities have I been resting on that were never the foundation?
Is my house built on the rock, or only on floors that have not yet been flooded?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the flood is showing me what I was really standing on, and not all of it was You. As the lesser authorities wash away, drive me down to the one foundation that cannot be moved. Let me stand on the rock, and not on the floors. Amen.

notes.primary: 1 Corinthians 3:11 (no other foundation than Jesus Christ); Matthew 7:24-25 (the house on the rock).
notes.tradition: The pivotal question of every upheaval — where now is the authority? — is Phyllis Tickle's, in The Great Emergence (2008), paraphrased and attributed, never quoted.

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: Personal and communal
figure: One body, members of one another
era: Why your upheaval is never only yours
moment:
This series holds two upheavals at once, because Scripture refuses to separate them. We are not isolated atoms who happen to gather on Sundays; Paul says we are one body, and individually members one of another. And in a body, nothing stays private. When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; when one is honored, all rejoice. The nerve runs the length of the whole frame.

So it is with upheaval. Your personal shaking ripples outward into your church; your church's shaking lands, eventually, in your own chest. The great reformations prove it both ways. Luther's private torment over a guilty conscience became a continent's earthquake. And the communal collapses — schisms, scandals, declines — break individual hearts one at a time. You cannot finally tell where the personal upheaval ends and the communal one begins, because in the body of Christ they were never two separate things.
voiceQuote: When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it. Or when one member is honored, all the members rejoice with it.
scriptureText: So we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another.
weight:
We are tempted to privatize our faith, and so to privatize our upheavals — to treat a crisis of belief as a solo event happening inside one skull, sealed off from the community. But there is no such thing as a sealed-off member. Your deconstruction changes the room you sit in on Sunday. Your renewal does too. And the health or sickness of your church seeps into your private prayers whether you invite it or not.

This is not a burden; it is a mercy. It means you do not have to carry your upheaval alone, and your church does not have to face its shaking with you watching from the outside. The same Spirit who is reforming you is reforming the body, and the body is meant to hold you while He does. So as this series walks the phases, it will always ask both questions — what is God doing in you, and what is He doing in the body — because the answer to one is never unrelated to the other.

upheaval.thePhase: This stands over all four phases. Personal and communal upheaval move through disconnect, disorientation, reorientation, and reconnect together — sometimes out of step, often pulling on each other. Naming both keeps you from the lie that your shaking is yours alone, or your church's is none of your concern.
upheaval.inYou: Your private upheaval is not as private as it feels. It is shaping the people around you even now, and they are shaping you. You are a member, not an island; your healing and your wounding both travel down the nerve to the whole body.
upheaval.inTheBody: When the church is shaken, individuals bleed — and when individuals are shaken, the church feels it whether it admits it or not. A healthy body does not ask its hurting members to suffer in private; it suffers with them, and it lets itself be changed by what it learns in the suffering.
upheaval.whatRemains: The body itself — one in Christ, members of one another. Arrangements within the body get shaken; the union does not. What cannot be shaken is that you belong to a whole, and the whole belongs to its Head.
reflection: Where have I been treating my upheaval as a private event sealed off from my community?
How is my church's shaking showing up in my own soul — or mine in mine?
Who in the body is suffering a shaking I have been watching from the outside?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You have made me a member, not an island. Teach me to bring my upheaval into the body instead of hiding it, and to feel my church's shaking as my own. Let the same Spirit who is reforming me reform us, and hold us to each other while You do. Amen.

notes.primary: 1 Corinthians 12:26 (when one member suffers, all suffer); Romans 12:5 (one body, members of one another).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: God is in the shaking
moment:
The deepest fear in any upheaval is not the shaking itself. It is the suspicion the shaking seems to prove: that God has gone. That if the ground were really His, it would not be moving — so the earthquake must mean abandonment. Psalm 46 walks straight up to that fear and stares it down. It pictures the absolute worst: the earth itself changing, the mountains — the most permanent things anyone could name — toppling into the heart of the sea, the waters roaring.

And then it refuses to be afraid. Not because the ground is steady; the psalm has just said it is not. The refusal rests on something else entirely: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Not a help once the trouble passes. A very present help in it. The God of Jacob is not the absence the quake seems to prove. He is the refuge standing in the middle of the wreckage, the one solid thing precisely when every solid thing is failing.
voiceQuote: God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore will we not be afraid, though the earth changes, though the mountains are shaken into the heart of the seas.
scriptureText: The LORD of Hosts is with us. The God of Jacob is our refuge.
weight:
Upheaval lies to us about God. It whispers that the shaking is evidence of His absence — that a present God would have held the mountains in place. But Psalm 46 reverses the logic completely. The mountains were never the refuge; they were only mountains, and mountains fall. God was always the refuge, and the day the mountains fall is the day you find out you were leaning on Him all along, or discover that you weren't.

This is the difference between an upheaval that destroys faith and one that deepens it. Both feel the same from inside — the same loss, the same vertigo. But one concludes God has left, and one concludes the mountains were never God. The second is the truth. He is a very present help in trouble, not after it. When everything you thought was solid is sliding into the sea, He has not gone anywhere. He is the refuge you can only find once the mountains are out of the way.

upheaval.thePhase: This is the word for disorientation above all — the phase where God seems most absent. The shaking is not proof He has left. He is the very present help in the trouble itself, the refuge you find precisely when the solid things fail.
upheaval.inYou: When your private world is sliding into the sea, the lie comes fast: God would have stopped this if He were here. He is here. He was never the mountains you were standing on; He is the refuge underneath them, and the quake is how you find Him.
upheaval.inTheBody: A shaken church is tempted to read its own instability as God's departure — the numbers falling, the certainties cracking, the ground moving. But the LORD of Hosts is with us is a plural promise, spoken to a community in upheaval. God does not abandon the church He is shaking; He is its refuge in the middle of the quake.
upheaval.whatRemains: God Himself — a very present help in trouble, the refuge that stands when the mountains fall. What cannot be shaken is not the ground beneath you but the One who is with you when the ground gives way.
reflection: What lie is my upheaval telling me about whether God is present?
Have I been leaning on mountains and calling them God?
Can I believe He is a very present help in the trouble, not only after it?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the shaking makes me doubt You are here, as if a present God would have held the mountains still. Be my refuge in the trouble, not only after it. When everything solid slides into the sea, let me find that You never moved. Amen.

notes.primary: Psalm 46:1-3, 7 (God is our refuge, though the mountains shake; the LORD of Hosts is with us).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: The refiner's fire
moment:
Malachi's picture of the coming God is not the one we expect. We brace for a judge with a gavel; what we get is a metalworker who pulls up a stool. He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver. The detail that he sits is the whole point — refining is patient work. The smith heats the ore and watches; as the metal melts, the impurities rise to the surface as a grey scum, and he draws them off; he heats it again, and again, until the surface goes so clear he can see his own face in it. Then he knows it is done.

That is what the fire of an upheaval is for. It is not God losing His temper and burning things down; it is God sitting down to refine. I have refined you, He says through Isaiah, but not as silver — I have chosen you in the furnace of affliction. The furnace is not the opposite of being chosen; it is the proof of it. The heat that feels like destruction is the heat that draws the dross to the surface so it can finally be taken away.
voiceQuote: He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi, and refine them as gold and silver.
scriptureText: Behold, I have refined you, but not as silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of affliction.
weight:
If you can believe the fire is a refiner's fire, everything about your upheaval changes — not the heat, but the meaning of the heat. Dross only rises when the metal is hot enough; the very thing that feels like ruin is the thing surfacing what needs to go. The impurities you never knew were in you — the false securities, the pride, the lukewarm compromises — do not appear in comfort. They appear in the furnace, where at last they can be drawn off.

And the refiner sits. He does not walk away and forget the crucible on the fire; he watches it the whole time, and he knows exactly how much heat the metal can take, and he stops the moment he can see his face in the surface. That is the promise hidden in the fire: it is measured, it is attended, and it has an end. He is refining you for a clarity you cannot reach any other way — until what reflects back from your life is the face of the One sitting at the fire.

upheaval.thePhase: The fire burns hottest in disconnect and disorientation — the painful early phases. Naming it as refining, not ruin, is what lets you stay in the furnace long enough for it to finish its work instead of bolting before the dross is drawn off.
upheaval.inYou: The upheaval is surfacing things in you that comfort kept hidden — and that is mercy, not cruelty. Do not waste the heat being only afraid of it. Let the dross rise and be taken; you are being refined toward a clarity you could not reach any softer way.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church in the furnace has its impurities surface too — the compromises, the idols, the rot that prosperity concealed. This is humiliating and it is purifying. The refiner is not destroying His church; He is drawing off what was never silver, so the real thing can shine.
upheaval.whatRemains: The refined metal — and the Refiner Himself, who sits and watches and will not overheat the crucible. What cannot be shaken is His attentive purpose: the fire is measured, it is for your good, and it has an end.
reflection: What is the heat of this upheaval surfacing in me that comfort had kept hidden?
Am I bolting from the furnace before the dross has been drawn off?
Can I trust that the Refiner is seated, watching, and will not overheat me?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have feared this fire as ruin when You meant it as refining. Sit at the crucible; draw off whatever in me was never silver. Give me the faith to stay in the heat until I reflect Your face, and the trust that You know exactly when it is enough. Amen.

notes.primary: Malachi 3:2-3 (he will sit as a refiner); Isaiah 48:10 (chosen in the furnace of affliction).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: A time to break down
moment:
When God commissions young Jeremiah, He gives him six verbs, and the order is not an accident. To pluck up, and to break down, and to destroy, and to overthrow — and then, only then, to build and to plant. Four verbs of demolition before two of construction. The prophet's first work is teardown, and the building waits behind it.

We hate this order. We want the building without the breaking, the new plant without the violence of pulling up the old roots. But the order is honest about how renewal actually works. You cannot raise a new structure on ground still occupied by the old one; the lot has to be cleared first. You cannot plant in soil still matted with the roots of what grew there before; the ground has to be broken. Ecclesiastes says it plainly — there is a time to break down, and a time to build up — and it does not pretend the second can come without the first.
voiceQuote: Behold, I have this day set you over the nations and over the kingdoms, to pluck up and to break down and to destroy and to overthrow, to build and to plant.
scriptureText: A time to break down, and a time to build up.
weight:
Much of the pain of an upheaval is that you are living in the gap between the verbs — after the breaking down, before the building up. The old structure is gone, the new one is not yet here, and it feels like nothing but loss, like destruction for its own sake. It is not. The demolition is the first half of a construction project; the cleared lot is the promise of a building you cannot see yet.

This does not make the teardown painless, and it does not give anyone license to wield the wrecking ball carelessly — Jeremiah's verbs were God's commission, not a mandate for every restless critic to smash what they dislike. But it does reframe the rubble. If God is in your upheaval, the breaking down is not the end of the story; it is the clearing of the ground. Live in the gap between the verbs as someone waiting for the building, not someone abandoned in the ruins.

upheaval.thePhase: These are the verbs of disconnect — pluck up, break down, destroy, overthrow — opening toward reorientation's build and plant. The teardown is real and it comes first; the gap between the verbs is the disorientation you have to live through to reach the building.
upheaval.inYou: If something in your life is being torn down — a structure of belief, a role, a way of being that no longer holds — do not assume it is only loss. The God who breaks down also builds. You may be living in the gap between the verbs, on a lot that has been cleared for something you cannot picture yet.
upheaval.inTheBody: Renewal in a church almost always begins with a teardown, and someone always grieves it. Wisdom discerns the difference between God's demolition, which clears the ground for building, and a restless person's wrecking ball, which smashes for the sake of smashing. The test is what comes after: God breaks down in order to build and to plant.
upheaval.whatRemains: The Builder behind the breaking. The wrecking and the raising are the same hand, with the same purpose. What cannot be shaken is that God never demolishes to leave a ruin; every teardown He authors is the first half of a building.
reflection: What is being torn down in my life right now — and can I believe it is clearing ground, not just loss?
Am I living in the gap between the verbs as someone waiting to build, or as someone abandoned in the rubble?
Where might I be swinging a wrecking ball God never put in my hand?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the breaking down is real, and I am living in the gap before the building. Help me trust that Your demolition clears the ground for what You will plant. Keep me from smashing what You meant to keep — and from despairing on a lot You are about to build on. Amen.

notes.primary: Jeremiah 1:10 (to pluck up and break down... to build and to plant); Ecclesiastes 3:3 (a time to break down, a time to build up).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: A heart of flesh
moment: We speak of a heart hardening as if it happened overnight. It does not. It happens the way limestone forms — one disappointment, one self-protection, one unanswered prayer at a time, each laid down so quietly you never feel the day you turned to stone. The cynicism was reasonable once. The armor kept out a real blade. The routine got you through a season you could not feel your way through. And then one morning you notice the prayers bounce off the inside of your own chest, and you cannot remember when you last felt anything in church but the schedule. Phyllis Tickle saw the same calcifying in the church itself — a hardened shell forming over a few centuries until the life inside is sealed off from the life outside. Ezekiel names the cure, and it is not effort. It is a transplant. The LORD promises to take out the stone Himself and put in a heart of flesh — soft, vulnerable, able to bleed and to feel again. You cannot soften your own heart any more than a stone can decide to beat. Which is why the upheaval comes. The breaking is the surgeon's incision, prying loose what would never have come out gently.
voiceQuote: A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you; and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh.
scriptureText: Tear your heart, and not your garments, and turn to the LORD, your God; for he is gracious and merciful, slow to anger, and abundant in lovingkindness.
weight: Notice what Joel asks for. Not torn garments — the visible, manageable, public grief that costs the heart nothing. He asks you to rend the heart itself, the inward tearing no one sees and no one can fake. We are endlessly willing to perform repentance with our clothing and our calendars while the stone stays exactly where it is. The upheaval refuses that bargain. It goes past the garments to the thing underneath, and the tearing it works in you is the only kind that reaches the stone. This is hard to receive as mercy, because nothing about it feels merciful while it is happening. The softening of a hardened heart is indistinguishable, from the inside, from being broken. But ask what the alternative is. A heart left to harden does not stay neutral; it goes on petrifying until nothing gets in and nothing gets out, until you are religious and untouchable and slowly dead. God loves you too much to leave you stone. So He does the thing you could never do to yourself, and it costs, and it is grace.

upheaval.thePhase: This is disconnect bleeding into disorientation — the early, surgical phase where God pries loose what hardened over years. It asks you to stop defending the stone. The shaking is not punishment; it is the incision that gets the petrified heart out so a living one can go in. Let it cut.
upheaval.inYou: Name the hardened places. The cynicism you call realism. The armor you built after the wound that should never have happened. The self-sufficiency that decided it was safer to need no one. These kept you alive once. Now they keep God out. The stone has to come, and it will not come gently.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church ossifies the same way a heart does — its forms hardening into a shell that holds the life out as much as in, until the structure survives and the tenderness is gone. When God removes the stony heart of an institution, it is painful and merciful at once. He is after a people soft to Him again, not a museum.
upheaval.whatRemains: The Surgeon and His intent. Hearts of stone are shakable; the One who removes them is not, and neither is His promise to give a heart of flesh. What cannot be shaken is that He is for your softening, not your ruin — even with the blade in His hand.
reflection: Where have I let my heart harden, and what was the wound that started the calcifying?
Am I offering God torn garments — visible, manageable grief — while the stone stays untouched?
Can I believe the breaking I am in is His surgery, not His abandonment?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I did not feel myself turning to stone, but I am stone, and I cannot soften myself. Take out what hardened over the years, even with the knife. Rend my heart, not just my garments. Give me a heart of flesh, tender to You again, whatever the cutting costs. Amen.

notes.primary: Ezekiel 36:26 (a new heart, the stony heart removed); Joel 2:13 (rend your heart, not your garments).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: Counting the cost
moment: Jesus does an odd thing for a man trying to gather a crowd. He tells them to do the math first. Which of you, wanting to build a tower, does not sit down and count the cost to see whether you can finish? He will not let anyone follow Him on a wave of feeling that has not reckoned with the price. Discipleship is a tower, and towers have a bill, and He would rather you count it now than abandon a half-built ruin later for everyone to mock. Upheaval has a bill too, and it always comes due. Centuries after that hillside, by the rivers of Babylon, the exiles learned exactly what their tower had cost. They sat down — the same posture Jesus named — and they wept, remembering the Zion they had lost. There is no pretending in that scene. No one tells them to cheer up because exile will work out for the good. They sit by the water and grieve what is gone, and the grief is not faithlessness. It is the honest invoice of an upheaval, read aloud and paid in tears. Scripture lets them weep without rebuke. It does not rush the mourning, and it does not pretend the loss was small.
voiceQuote: Which of you, desiring to build a tower, doesn't first sit down and count the cost, to see if he has enough to complete it?
scriptureText: By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down. Yes, we wept, when we remembered Zion.
weight: We are bad at this. We want the upheaval without the bill — the new life without grieving the old one, the deconstruction without the loss of the people who deconstructed differently, the move of God without counting what the move costs. And so we either refuse to begin, or we begin pretending it is free, and the unpaid grief ambushes us later with interest. Counting the cost is not the opposite of faith; it is faith with its eyes open. You are allowed to sit down by the river. You are allowed to weep for what the shaking is taking — the relationships that will not survive it, the certainties you cannot get back, the version of yourself you are losing and quietly loved. None of that mourning is unbelief. The exiles wept and were still God's people; their tears were on the way to a return they could not yet see. Grieve the cost honestly. The upheaval that gets mourned is the one you can actually walk through; the one you pretend is painless is the one that breaks you in the dark.

upheaval.thePhase: This is disconnect bleeding into disorientation — the break has happened, and now the bill arrives. The phase asks you to count the cost honestly and to grieve what it takes, without ever calling that grief a failure of faith. You are meant to sit by the river before you find the road.
upheaval.inYou: Honor what your shaking costs. The relationships, the securities, the certainties, the self you are losing — these are real losses, and you are allowed to sit down and weep for them. Counting the cost is not weakness or unbelief. It is the honesty that lets you carry the loss instead of being ambushed by it.
upheaval.inTheBody: A reforming church pays real prices. People leave. Treasured things are set down. The old comfort dies, even when the change is right. Pretending the reformation is painless is a lie that wounds the grieving twice. A wise community counts the cost out loud and mourns what it loses, and is healthier for the honesty.
upheaval.whatRemains: The God who outlasts the bill. Everything the upheaval charges you was shakable; the One you are following through it is not. What cannot be shaken is that the cost, however steep, is paid toward Him — and He is worth the tower.
reflection: What is this upheaval actually costing me, named plainly and not minimized?
Am I pretending the loss is small to avoid the grief I am afraid to feel?
Can I sit by the river and weep without calling my own tears a failure of faith?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have been pretending this cost me nothing, and it has cost me much. Let me sit by the river and grieve what the shaking took, without calling my tears unbelief. Help me count the cost with open eyes, and follow You anyway, all the way to the far side. Amen.

notes.primary: Luke 14:28 (count the cost); Psalm 137:1 (by the rivers of Babylon, we wept).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: The pull back to Egypt
figure: We wish we had died in Egypt
moment: It does not take long. Weeks, maybe — barely past the parted sea, the water still drying on their sandals — and Israel is already homesick for slavery. We wish we had died in Egypt by the flesh-pots, they cry, where we sat and ate our fill of bread. Listen to what nostalgia does to the memory. It keeps the flesh-pots and quietly deletes the whips. By Numbers it has gotten even more vivid and more absurd: they remember the fish they ate for nothing, the cucumbers, the melons, the leeks, the onions, the garlic — a slave's menu recalled as a feast. For nothing, they say, as though slavery were generosity, as though their masters had been feeding them out of love rather than working them to keep them strong. This is the strange power of the wilderness. It makes Egypt look good. The in-between place is so disorienting, so stripped of the old familiar fullness, that the mind goes hunting backward for comfort and finds it in the very bondage God just tore them out of. They are not lying, exactly. They really do remember the melons. They have simply forgotten the chains that came with them.
voiceQuote: We wish that we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the flesh-pots and ate our fill of bread; for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger.
scriptureText: We remember the fish, which we ate in Egypt for nothing; the cucumbers, and the melons, and the leeks, and the onions, and the garlic.
weight: The wilderness will do this to you. Somewhere in the disorientation — when the new thing has not arrived and the old thing is irretrievably gone — you will catch yourself idealizing the exact bondage God broke you out of. The old certainty that answered every question, even though it was answering them falsely. The old relationship that was killing you slowly, remembered now as warmth. The old self that was at least familiar, even if it was not free. Nostalgia is the wilderness talking, and the wilderness lies. It tells you Egypt was better. It was not. You are remembering the cucumbers and forgetting the chains. The test is simple and brutal: if you actually went back, you would not get the melons. You would get the whips again, because the melons were always the bait on the bondage. The way through an upheaval is forward, through the wilderness, hard as that is — not back into the house of slavery dressed up by memory as home. Do not trust the homesickness. It is pointing you toward Egypt, and Egypt is not where God is going.

upheaval.thePhase: This is disorientation in full — the wilderness between the old life and the new, where bearings are gone and the mind goes hunting backward. The phase asks you to refuse the pull of nostalgia, to recognize the longing for Egypt as the wilderness talking, and to keep facing forward when going back feels like relief.
upheaval.inYou: You will be tempted to idealize the very thing God broke you out of — the old certainty, the old relationship, the old self. The wilderness whispers that Egypt was better, warmer, safer. It was not. You are remembering the cucumbers and forgetting the chains. Do not trust the homesickness; it points the wrong way.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church in transition aches for the way it used to be — the fuller pews, the settled certainties, the old familiar feeling of belonging. But the longing for Egypt is not a call from God; it is the wilderness talking. The road is forward, through what is uncomfortable, not back into a bondage memory has dressed up as home.
upheaval.whatRemains: The God going forward, not back. The wilderness shakes your bearings and your memory; the One leading through it does not change. What cannot be shaken is that He is ahead of you, in the unfamiliar country — never behind you, in the Egypt you are tempted to crawl back toward.
reflection: What bondage is my memory quietly dressing up as something I miss?
Which chains am I forgetting when I remember the cucumbers of the old life?
Is my homesickness pointing me forward through the wilderness, or backward into Egypt?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, the wilderness is making my old bondage look like home, and I am aching to go back. Remind me of the chains I am forgetting. Keep me facing forward when going back feels like relief. You are ahead of me, not behind me. Lead me through, not back. Amen.

notes.primary: Exodus 16:3 (we wish we had died in Egypt by the flesh-pots); Numbers 11:5 (we remember the fish, the cucumbers, the melons).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: Discontent and grumbling
moment: Two people stand in the same congregation, both deeply dissatisfied, both saying this cannot go on. From the outside they are identical — the same heat, the same refusal to accept what is. But their roots run in opposite directions, and the fruit will not be the same. Bill Hybels gave one of them a name: holy discontent, the God-given ache that refuses what is wrong and drives a person toward God and toward repair. It is the fire that lit the prophets and the reformers, a sacred unwillingness to make peace with what should not be. The other is older and uglier, and Numbers shows it catching alight. The people were as murmurers, speaking evil in the ears of the LORD; and when He heard it, His anger was kindled, and fire broke out and burned in the edges of the camp. Same dissatisfaction. Opposite direction. Holy discontent moves toward God; grumbling festers against Him. One drives you to your knees and then to your feet to build; the other only mutters in the tent and corrodes. Paul names the second plainly and tells the Philippians to have none of it: do all things without murmurings. The surface looks the same. The roots could not be more different.
voiceQuote: The people were as murmurers, speaking evil in the ears of the LORD; and when the LORD heard it, his anger was kindled.
voiceAttribution: From the book of Numbers — Numbers 11:1 (WEB)
scriptureText: Do all things without murmurings and disputes.
weight: So examine the dissatisfaction in you, because not all of it is holy, and the wrong kind disguises itself as the right. Ask which way it runs. Holy discontent is restless toward God and toward action — it cannot abide the wrong, and it moves you to do something faithful about it. It builds. Grumbling is restless against — it nurses the grievance, assigns the blame, and moves you toward bitterness and toward no one's good. It burns. The same heat fuels both, which is exactly why you can mistake one for the other and call your own corrosion a prophetic gift. The honest test is direction and fruit. Does your complaint drive you to pray, to repair, to act toward what is right? Or does it only drive you to mutter, to recruit allies for your resentment, to set quiet fires in the edges of the camp? One is the Spirit's ignition for renewal. The other is the murmuring that drew fire in the wilderness. Learn the difference in your own chest before it costs you, or the camp, more than you meant to spend.

upheaval.thePhase: This is disconnect, where renewal ignites — and where the ignition has to be discerned. The phase asks you to tell the holy discontent that drives toward God and repair from the grumbling that festers against Him and corrodes. Same heat; opposite roots. Discern which fire you are carrying before you act on it.
upheaval.inYou: Examine your dissatisfaction. Is it holy discontent — a sacred ache that moves you toward God and toward faithful action? Or is it grumbling — a corrosive muttering that moves you away from Him and toward bitterness? Same heat, opposite roots. The test is direction: does it build, or does it only burn?
upheaval.inTheBody: Every reformation began in discontent; so did every pointless split that helped no one. A community has to learn the prophet's holy discontent, which builds, from the murmurer's grumbling, which only burns. One is the Spirit's ignition for renewal. The other is fire set in the edges of the camp, and it consumes the people who light it.
upheaval.whatRemains: The Spirit who ignites the holy fire. Discontent and grumbling both shake a community; the One who lights the sacred kind does not waver. What cannot be shaken is that God still ignites holy discontent in His people — and still calls the murmuring what it is.
reflection: Which way does my dissatisfaction run — toward God and repair, or against Him and toward bitterness?
Am I calling my own corrosive grumbling a prophetic gift?
Where am I setting quiet fires in the edges of the camp instead of building?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, my heart is full of dissatisfaction, and I cannot always tell the holy kind from the corrosive. Show me which fire I am carrying. Kindle the discontent that drives me toward You and toward repair, and put out the murmuring that only burns. Keep me from setting fires in the camp. Amen.

notes.primary: Numbers 11:1 (the people murmured and the LORD's anger was kindled); Philippians 2:14 (do all things without murmurings).
notes.tradition: Builds on Bill Hybels' concept of holy discontent (Holy Discontent, 2007), paraphrased and attributed, distinguishing it from corrosive grumbling.

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: He tears and He heals
figure: The God who wounds and binds
moment: Hosea says something that should stop us where we stand. Come, and let us return to the LORD; for He has torn, and He will heal us; He has struck, and He will bind us up. Read it slowly. The same God who tore us is the One who will heal. The hand that struck is the hand that binds the wound. This is not an enemy's blade followed by a stranger's mercy; it is one hand, doing both. We have a name for this and mostly refuse to believe it: severe mercy. Love, when nothing softer will reach us, sometimes takes the form of a wound. Job, who had every cause to read his suffering as abandonment, says the same and refuses the easier conclusion: He wounds, and binds up; He injures, and His hands make whole. Both verbs belong to God. We want to assign the tearing to the devil, to chance, to our enemies, and keep only the binding for Him. Scripture will not let us split Him in two. The tearing is not the opposite of His love. Sometimes, when no gentler thing could reach the place that needed reaching, the tearing is the form His love is forced to take.
voiceQuote: Come, and let us return to the LORD; for he has torn, and he will heal us; he has struck, and he will bind us up.
scriptureText: For he wounds, and binds up; he injures, and his hands make whole.
weight: Everything turns on who you think holds the knife. If the wound of your upheaval came from an enemy, the only sane response is to flee — to run from the source of the pain as fast as you can. But Hosea reframes the whole scene. If God is in your upheaval, then the wound is not abandonment; it is the first half of a healing not yet finished. And that changes the direction you should run. You do not flee the One who tore you; you return to Him, because the hand that tore is the only hand that can bind. This is the hardest turn in the life of faith — to move toward the source of the wound rather than away from it, trusting that the One who struck means to make you whole. Flee, and the wound stays open, infected by your fear that God has become your enemy. Return, and the same hand that opened it begins to close it. The mercy is in this: He tears the ones He means to heal, and He waits to bind up everyone willing to come back.

upheaval.thePhase: This is disconnect bleeding into disorientation — the wounded, bewildering early phase, reframed. The wound is God's, and so is the healing. The phase asks you to read the tearing as severe mercy rather than rejection, and to turn back toward the One who struck, because His is the only hand that binds.
upheaval.inYou: If God is in your upheaval, the wound is not abandonment — it is the first half of a healing. The hand that tore you is the only hand that can bind you up. So do not flee Him in your pain; return to Him. Moving toward the source of the wound, not away, is how the wound finally closes.
upheaval.inTheBody: A church can endure God's tearing — a humbling, a stripping, a hard discipline — and read it as His rejection, His divorce papers served. Hosea reframes it: He tears the people He means to heal. The shaking of a church He loves is severe mercy, not abandonment, and the way back to wholeness runs toward Him, not away.
upheaval.whatRemains: The wounding-and-binding hand. The tearing shakes everything; the One whose hand both strikes and heals does not change. What cannot be shaken is that the wound and the healing come from the same love — and that He waits to bind up all who return.
reflection: Whose hand do I believe holds the knife in my upheaval — an enemy's, or the One who means to heal me?
Am I fleeing the wound, and so fleeing the only hand that can bind it?
Can I read this tearing as severe mercy rather than as God's rejection?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, I have read this wound as abandonment and been running from You. But the hand that tore me is the only hand that can heal me. Teach me to turn back toward You instead of away. Bind up what You have torn, and let me trust the mercy hidden in the wound. Amen.

notes.primary: Hosea 6:1 (he has torn and he will heal); Job 5:18 (he wounds and binds up).

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: Appointed seasons
figure: The God who changes the times
moment:
When the kings of the earth seemed to be the only powers that mattered, Daniel said something that put them all in their place: it is God who changes the times and the seasons; He removes kings and sets up kings. The rise of one empire and the fall of another, which looked to everyone else like raw history happening, was the work of a hand on the calendar. Centuries later Paul stands on the Areopagus and says it to a city full of philosophers: the God who made every nation from one blood has determined the appointed seasons, and the very bounds of where they would live. Nothing is loose. Nothing is unscheduled.

Upheaval almost always feels like the opposite of this. It feels like chaos slipping its leash, like the times running wild. But Scripture keeps insisting that the seasons are appointed, not accidental. The roughly five-hundred-year beat that Phyllis Tickle traced in the church's great rummage sales is, on this reading, not history misbehaving. It is the rhythm of the God who governs the times, renewing His people on a schedule He set before any of them were born.
voiceQuote: He changes the times and the seasons; he removes kings, and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise, and knowledge to those who have understanding.
scriptureText: He made from one blood every nation of men to dwell on all the surface of the earth, having determined appointed seasons, and the bounds of their habitation.
weight:
There is a particular terror in believing your upheaval is random — that it fell on you out of a meaningless sky, signifying nothing, answerable to no one. If that were true, the only sane response would be to brace and endure. But it is not true. Your shaking did not catch God off guard, and it is not happening in a vacuum where meaning has drained away. He changes times and seasons; this season of yours is one He appointed, and appointed seasons have edges.

That is the quiet mercy of the word season. A season is bounded. It came in on a date and it will go out on one, and the One who set both is not anxious about either. You may not be able to see the calendar; you are not meant to. But there is a hand on it, and the hand belongs to the God who has done this before and will do it again on time. Your upheaval is not loose in the world. It is held.

upheaval.thePhase: This word spans all four phases. Disconnect, disorientation, reorientation, reconnect — none of them arrive by accident, and none of them outlast the season God appointed for them. What it asks is trust: to believe the shaking is scheduled, bounded, and governed, even when it looks like the times have come unhinged.
upheaval.inYou: Your private shaking did not slip past God on its way to you. He changes the times and the seasons, and this one is yours for now, not forever. It has a beginning He knew and an end He has already set. There is a hand on the calendar, and it is steadier than yours.
upheaval.inTheBody: The church's great upheavals recur with an almost seasonal beat — every few centuries the hardened shell cracks and the rummage sale comes round again. Read rightly, this is not decline running wild. It is the God who appoints the seasons renewing His church on time, as He has done before and will do again.
upheaval.whatRemains: The God who governs the times. Empires change, seasons turn, the calendar runs on; the hand that moves it does not. What cannot be shaken is that the One appointing your season is Himself outside all seasons, unhurried and unchanging.
reflection: Where have I been treating my upheaval as random chaos rather than an appointed season?
What would change if I believed this season had both an edge and a Hand on the calendar?
Can I trust the God who changes the times to be unanxious about mine?
upheaval.prayer: Lord, You change the times and the seasons, and this hard one is somehow on Your calendar. When it feels like chaos slipping its leash, remind me there is a Hand on it. Hold me through the season You appointed, until You bring it, on time, to its end. Amen.

notes.primary: Daniel 2:21 (he changes the times and seasons); Acts 17:26 (having determined appointed seasons).
notes.tradition: Resonant with Phyllis Tickle's roughly-500-year rummage-sale rhythm (The Great Emergence, 2008, crediting Mark Dyer), paraphrased and attributed — read here as God's appointed seasons, not chaos.

volumeSubtitle: Why God shakes what He loves
title: A kingdom that cannot be shaken
moment:
On the first day this series named the promise from its dark side: what can be shaken is shaken so that what cannot be shaken may remain. Now turn the same verse over and read the bright side.
